question: A licensee is trying to determine whether an item left by the seller is a fixture (real property) or personal property. Which set of factors, often remembered by the mnemonic MARIA, is used to make this determination?
choice_a: Method of attachment, adaptability to the property's use, relationship of the parties, intention of the annexor, and agreement between the parties
choice_b: Market value, appraised condition, replacement cost, insurance status, and age of the item
choice_c: Location on the lot, mortgage terms, appraisal date, resale value, and assessed value
choice_d: Original purchase price, brand, warranty status, installation date, and manufacturer
explanation: Whether an item is a fixture is judged by MARIA: Method of attachment, Adaptability to the real property's use, Relationship between the parties, Intention of the annexor, and any Agreement between the parties. Items meeting the fixture test convey with the real property unless excluded by contract.
source_note: National real property law principle — fixture test (MARIA), universally taught in U.S. real estate pre-licensing curricula.

question: A tenant operating a bakery in a rented retail space installs a large commercial oven bolted to the floor. At the end of the lease, who is generally entitled to remove the oven?
choice_a: The landlord, because anything bolted down automatically becomes real property
choice_b: The tenant, because it is a trade fixture installed for conducting business
choice_c: Neither party, because the item must remain in place permanently once installed
choice_d: The tenant's lender, because the oven secures the tenant's business loan
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a tenant attaches to a rented space for use in a trade or business. Despite being attached, they remain the tenant's personal property and must generally be removed by the end of the lease term, with the tenant responsible for repairing any damage from removal.
source_note: National real property law principle — trade fixture exception to the general fixture rule.

question: A farmer sells a parcel of land while an unharvested corn crop is still growing. Under general real property principles, how is the growing corn crop classified?
choice_a: A fixture that automatically transfers with the land to the buyer
choice_b: An encumbrance on the title
choice_c: Emblements, treated as personal property belonging to the party entitled to harvest it
explanation: Annual cultivated crops (fructus industriales), called emblements, are treated as personal property even though they are attached to the land, because they result from a person's labor rather than being a natural part of the land itself.
source_note: National real property law principle — emblements as personal property.

question: When a seller conveys the riding lawn mower and patio furniture to the buyer along with the home, what legal document is used to transfer title to these items?
choice_a: A deed
choice_b: A certificate of title
choice_c: A lien release
explanation: A bill of sale is the instrument used to transfer ownership of personal property. A deed conveys title to real property; personal property being included in a sale is documented and transferred separately via a bill of sale.
source_note: National conveyancing principle — bill of sale vs. deed distinction.

question: A homeowner has a built-in dishwasher professionally installed and wired into the kitchen cabinetry. When the home is later sold, what happens to the dishwasher unless the sales contract states otherwise?
choice_a: It conveys with the home as a fixture, since it is permanently attached and adapted to the property's use
choice_b: It remains the seller's personal property and must be removed before closing
choice_c: It becomes the buyer's property only if separately purchased at closing
choice_d: It reverts to the appliance manufacturer under warranty law
explanation: Because the dishwasher is permanently attached (built into the cabinetry and wired in) and adapted for use in the home, it satisfies the fixture test and is presumed to convey with the real property unless the contract specifically excludes it.
source_note: National real property law principle — application of the fixture test to built-in appliances.

question: A legal description begins 'Commencing at the point of beginning, thence north 100 feet, thence east 150 feet, thence south 100 feet, thence west 150 feet to the point of beginning.' Which method of legal description is being used?
choice_a: Lot and block
choice_b: Metes and bounds
choice_c: Government (rectangular) survey
explanation: Metes and bounds descriptions trace a property's boundaries using compass directions and distances starting and ending at a fixed point of beginning (POB), and the description must always close back on the POB.
source_note: National legal description method — metes and bounds, universally tested land description type.

question: A property is legally described as 'Lot 14, Block 3, Sunnyside Estates Subdivision, as recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 47.' Which method of legal description does this represent?
choice_a: Metes and bounds
choice_b: Government rectangular survey
choice_c: Lot and block
explanation: The lot and block (recorded plat) system identifies a parcel by referencing a lot and block number shown on a subdivision plat map that has been officially recorded with the county, along with the recording book and page.
source_note: National legal description method — lot and block/recorded plat system.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, what two reference lines intersect to establish the starting point for measuring townships and ranges in a given survey area?
choice_a: A section line and a quarter-section line
choice_b: A metes and bounds line and a monument line
choice_c: A plat line and a lot line
choice_d: A principal meridian (running north-south) and a base line (running east-west)
explanation: The government survey system is built around principal meridians, which run north-south, and base lines, which run east-west. Their intersection is the reference point from which townships (measured north/south in tiers) and ranges (measured east/west) are located.
source_note: National legal description method — government/rectangular survey reference lines.

question: In the government rectangular survey system, a standard township is best described as:
choice_a: A square parcel of land 6 miles by 6 miles, containing 36 sections
choice_b: A square parcel of land 1 mile by 1 mile, containing 640 acres
choice_c: A strip of land running the full width of a state
explanation: A township is a 6-mile by 6-mile square (36 square miles) subdivided into 36 numbered sections, each 1 mile square. Townships are the basic building block of the government survey grid.
source_note: National legal description method — township size in the government survey system.

question: Under the government rectangular survey system, one standard section of land contains how many acres?
choice_a: 36 acres
choice_b: 640 acres
choice_c: 160 acres
explanation: A section is one square mile of land, which equals 640 acres. There are 36 sections in each 6-mile by 6-mile township.
source_note: National legal description method — section size (640 acres) in the government survey system.

question: In the government rectangular survey system, which statement correctly distinguishes range lines from township lines?
choice_a: Range lines and township lines both run diagonally to form 45-degree survey grids
choice_b: Township lines are used only in metes and bounds surveys, not rectangular surveys
choice_c: Range lines run north-south and are numbered east or west of the principal meridian, while township lines run east-west and are numbered north or south of the base line
choice_d: Range lines mark county boundaries and township lines mark state boundaries
explanation: Range lines run north-south, spaced 6 miles apart, and are numbered east or west of the principal meridian. Township lines run east-west, also spaced 6 miles apart, and are numbered north or south of the base line. Together they form the township/range grid used to identify a specific township.
source_note: National legal description method — range lines vs. township lines in the government survey system.

question: When an appraiser or agent measures the gross living area (GLA) of a single-family home, which standard measurement approach is used?
choice_a: Interior dimensions of every room including closets and hallways only
choice_b: The total footprint of the lot, including the yard
choice_c: The volume of the structure measured in cubic feet
choice_d: Exterior dimensions of the finished, above-grade living space
explanation: Gross living area is standardly measured using the exterior dimensions of the finished, heated/cooled living space located above grade, providing a consistent basis for comparing homes in the sales comparison approach.
source_note: National measurement standard — exterior-dimension method for gross living area.

question: For purposes of land measurement calculations, one acre is equal to how many square feet?
choice_a: 43,560 square feet
choice_b: 36,000 square feet
choice_c: 5,280 square feet
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet. This conversion factor is used whenever converting between acreage and square footage in land measurement problems.
source_note: National land measurement standard — acre-to-square-feet conversion.

question: A section of land contains 640 acres. How many acres are in the NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of that section?
choice_a: 160 acres
choice_b: 40 acres
choice_c: 80 acres
explanation: Multiply the fractions and apply them to the 640-acre section: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16, and 640 acres ÷ 16 = 40 acres. The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of a section always equals 40 acres.
source_note: National land measurement calculation — aliquot part of a section.

question: Which statement best defines a lien as it relates to real property?
choice_a: A written promise to convey title at a future date
choice_b: A right to physically occupy another's land for a stated period
choice_c: A claim or charge against property that serves as security for the payment of a debt or obligation
choice_d: A restriction on the architectural style of future improvements
explanation: A lien is an encumbrance that gives a creditor a legal claim against a property as security for a debt. If the debt is not paid, the lienholder may be able to force a sale of the property to satisfy the obligation.
source_note: National encumbrance law — definition of a lien.

question: A court enters a judgment against a debtor. This judgment lien attaches to which of the debtor's property?
choice_a: Only the single specific parcel named in the lawsuit, because it is a specific lien
choice_b: Only personal property, never real property
choice_c: Only property acquired before the debt was incurred
choice_d: All real property the debtor owns or later acquires in the county where the judgment is recorded, because it is a general lien
explanation: A judgment lien is a general lien, meaning it attaches to all real (and sometimes personal) property owned by the debtor within the jurisdiction, as opposed to a specific lien, such as a mortgage, which attaches only to a particular, identified parcel.
source_note: National encumbrance law — general lien vs. specific lien distinction.

question: A contractor who performs unpaid work on a home may file a lien against the property. This is known as a:
choice_a: Mechanic's lien
choice_b: Estate lien
choice_c: Easement lien
explanation: A mechanic's lien protects contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers who provide labor or materials to improve real property but are not paid. It is a specific, involuntary lien against the improved property.
source_note: National encumbrance law — mechanic's lien.

question: Compared to a previously recorded mortgage lien, an unpaid real property tax lien generally has which priority?
choice_a: The mortgage lien always takes priority because it was recorded first
choice_b: The tax lien takes superior priority over the mortgage lien regardless of recording date
choice_c: Both liens are paid on a pro-rata basis regardless of type
choice_d: Tax liens are subordinate to all privately recorded liens
explanation: Real property tax liens are generally given superior priority over other liens, including previously recorded mortgages, because government taxing authority claims take precedence to ensure tax revenue collection.
source_note: National encumbrance law — priority of property tax liens.

question: A driveway easement allows the owner of Lot A to cross Lot B to reach the street. Lot A benefits from the easement and Lot B is burdened by it. This type of easement is called:
choice_a: An easement in gross, because it benefits a specific individual rather than land
choice_b: A license, because it can be revoked at any time
choice_c: An easement appurtenant, because it involves a dominant tenement (Lot A) and a servient tenement (Lot B) and runs with the land
choice_d: An encroachment, because a structure crosses the boundary line
explanation: An easement appurtenant requires two parcels: a dominant tenement that benefits from the easement (Lot A) and a servient tenement that is burdened by it (Lot B). This type of easement runs with the land and transfers automatically when either property is sold.
source_note: National encumbrance law — easement appurtenant.

question: A utility company holds the right to run power lines across a landowner's property. Because this right benefits the utility company rather than benefiting an adjoining parcel of land, it is best classified as:
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: A license
choice_c: An easement by prescription
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or entity (such as a utility company) rather than a neighboring parcel of land, so there is no dominant tenement — only a servient tenement that is burdened by the easement.
source_note: National encumbrance law — easement in gross.

question: A rear parcel has no access to a public road except by crossing a neighboring lot. A court may grant the rear parcel's owner a legal right to cross the neighboring lot. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement by necessity
choice_b: An easement by prescription
choice_c: A license
explanation: An easement by necessity is created when a parcel is landlocked and has no other legal means of access, giving the owner a court-recognized right to cross an adjoining parcel to reach a public road.
source_note: National encumbrance law — easement by necessity.

question: A homeowner gives a neighbor casual permission to walk across the backyard as a shortcut to a nearby park. This type of permission is best classified as a:
choice_a: Easement appurtenant, which runs with the land
choice_b: License, which is a revocable, personal permission to use land and is not considered an interest in real property
choice_c: Easement by necessity, since it provides access to a public place
choice_d: Encroachment, since the neighbor is physically on the land
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use another's land. Unlike an easement, it is not an interest in real property, does not run with the land, and can typically be revoked at any time by the property owner or ends upon sale of the property.
source_note: National encumbrance law — license distinguished from an easement.

question: A property survey reveals that a neighbor's garage extends two feet over the boundary line onto the subject property. This condition is known as:
choice_a: An easement
choice_b: A license
choice_c: An encroachment
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement, such as a garage, fence, or driveway, extends over a property's boundary line onto an adjoining owner's land. Encroachments are typically discovered through a survey and can cloud title.
source_note: National encumbrance law — encroachment.

question: Which set of conditions must generally be satisfied for a person to acquire legal title to another's land through adverse possession?
choice_a: Possession that is secret, sporadic, and permitted by the true owner
choice_b: Payment of one year's property taxes only, regardless of possession
choice_c: A written lease agreement recorded for at least five years
choice_d: Possession that is open and notorious, continuous for the statutory period, hostile to the true owner's title, and actual and exclusive
explanation: Adverse possession generally requires possession that is open and notorious (obvious, not hidden), continuous for the state's statutory period, hostile/adverse to the true owner's interest (without permission), and actual and exclusive possession of the property.
source_note: National encumbrance/title law — elements of adverse possession.

question: A landowner sells the subsurface mineral rights to an energy company while retaining ownership of the surface. This is possible because:
choice_a: Mineral rights can be severed from the surface estate and conveyed or leased separately
choice_b: Mineral rights automatically transfer with any deed regardless of intent
choice_c: Only government entities may hold mineral rights
choice_d: Mineral rights cannot legally be separated from surface ownership
explanation: Ownership of real property can be divided vertically: the surface estate and the subsurface (mineral) estate can be owned separately. A landowner may sell, lease, or retain mineral rights independently of the surface rights.
source_note: National property rights principle — severance of mineral rights.

question: An owner whose land borders a flowing river has certain rights to make reasonable use of the adjacent water. These rights are known as:
choice_a: Littoral rights
choice_b: Riparian rights
choice_c: Avulsion rights
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream, and generally give the owner reasonable use of the water. (Littoral rights, by contrast, apply to land bordering non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes or oceans.)
source_note: National property rights principle — riparian water rights.

question: The right to use, develop, or lease the space above a parcel of land, separate from the surface rights, is known as:
choice_a: Riparian rights
choice_b: Subsurface rights
choice_c: Air rights
explanation: Air rights allow the space above a parcel to be used, developed, or transferred separately from the surface, such as when a developer purchases air rights to build over an existing structure or transfers development rights to another parcel.
source_note: National property rights principle — air rights as a separately conveyable interest.

question: A life estate is granted 'to Maria for the life of her mother, Elena.' If Maria dies before Elena, what happens to the life estate?
choice_a: The life estate ends immediately upon Maria's death
choice_b: The property automatically passes in fee simple to Maria's heirs
choice_c: The grantor regains full title immediately upon Maria's death
choice_d: The life estate continues, held by Maria's heirs or successors, until Elena dies, because this is a life estate pur autre vie
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant (here, Elena). If the life tenant (Maria) dies first, the estate does not terminate — it passes to Maria's heirs or estate and continues until the measuring life (Elena) ends.
source_note: National estate law — life estate pur autre vie.

question: A grantor conveys a life estate to her uncle and specifies that upon the uncle's death, title will pass to a named charity. The charity's future interest is called a:
choice_a: Remainder interest
choice_b: Reversion interest
choice_c: Leasehold interest
explanation: When a life estate is created and the future interest is designated to pass to a third party (rather than back to the original grantor), that third party holds a remainder interest. If instead the property were to return to the grantor, the grantor would hold a reversion interest.
source_note: National estate law — remainder vs. reversion interests following a life estate.

question: A single individual purchases a home and takes title in her name alone, with no co-owners. This form of ownership is known as:
choice_a: Tenancy in common
choice_b: Ownership in severalty
choice_c: Joint tenancy
explanation: Ownership in severalty means title is held by one person or legal entity alone, 'severed' from ownership by anyone else. It is the simplest and most complete form of sole ownership.
source_note: National ownership forms — severalty (sole ownership).

question: Three unrelated investors purchase a property together, each holding a different percentage interest, with no right of survivorship among them. This form of co-ownership is:
choice_a: Joint tenancy
choice_b: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: Tenancy in common
explanation: Tenancy in common allows two or more owners to hold undivided interests in a property, which may be unequal in size, with no right of survivorship. Each co-tenant may sell, transfer, or will their individual interest independently.
source_note: National ownership forms — tenancy in common.

question: Two siblings take title to a property as joint tenants with right of survivorship. For a valid joint tenancy to exist, the co-owners must share which four unities?
choice_a: Marriage, title, income, and possession
choice_b: Time, marriage, deed, and mortgage
choice_c: Title, appraisal, escrow, and recording
explanation: A valid joint tenancy requires the four unities: time (interests acquired at the same time), title (acquired via the same document), interest (equal shares), and possession (equal right to use the whole property). Joint tenancy also carries the right of survivorship.
source_note: National ownership forms — joint tenancy and the four unities.

question: A married couple takes title to their home in a form of ownership available only to legally married spouses, under which neither spouse may convey their interest without the other's consent, and the interest passes automatically to the surviving spouse. This is:
choice_a: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_b: Tenancy in common
choice_c: Ownership in severalty
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership available only to married spouses. It includes a right of survivorship, and generally neither spouse can convey or encumber the property without the other's consent, offering additional protection from the debts of one spouse alone.
source_note: National ownership forms — tenancy by the entirety.

question: In a condominium, an individual unit owner's interest in the property typically consists of:
choice_a: Shares of stock in a corporation that owns the entire building
choice_b: Fee simple ownership of the individual unit, combined with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the common areas
choice_c: A leasehold interest in the unit only, with no ownership interest in common areas
choice_d: A life estate in the unit that terminates upon sale
explanation: Condominium ownership combines fee simple title to the individual unit's airspace with an undivided percentage interest, held as tenants in common with the other unit owners, in the building's common areas and elements.
source_note: National common-interest ownership forms — condominium ownership structure.

question: In a housing cooperative, a resident does not directly own real property. Instead, the resident typically owns:
choice_a: A fee simple deed to the specific unit occupied
choice_b: An easement appurtenant to the building
choice_c: Shares of stock in the cooperative corporation, paired with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
choice_d: A life estate in the entire building
explanation: In a cooperative, a corporation holds title to the entire building. Residents purchase shares of stock in that corporation, which entitle them to a proprietary lease giving them the right to occupy a specific unit — they do not hold direct real property title to their unit.
source_note: National common-interest ownership forms — cooperative ownership structure.

question: A buyer purchases the right to use a beachfront condominium unit for one specific week every year, sharing ownership or use rights with other buyers who use the unit during other weeks. This arrangement is known as:
choice_a: A cooperative interest
choice_b: A tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: A life estate pur autre vie
explanation: A timeshare divides the use or ownership of a property, typically a vacation property, among multiple buyers, each of whom obtains the right to use the property during a designated recurring time period each year.
source_note: National common-interest ownership forms — timeshare ownership.

question: A property owner transfers legal title to real estate to a trustee, who manages the property for the benefit of a named beneficiary. Under this arrangement, who holds legal title versus equitable/beneficial title?
choice_a: The trustee holds legal title while the beneficiary holds equitable (beneficial) title
choice_b: The beneficiary holds legal title while the trustee holds equitable title
choice_c: Both parties hold identical, undivided legal title
choice_d: Neither party holds title until the trust terminates
explanation: In a trust arrangement, the trustee holds legal title to the property and has a fiduciary duty to manage it according to the trust's terms, while the beneficiary holds equitable (beneficial) title and receives the benefits of the property.
source_note: National ownership forms — property held in trust (trustee vs. beneficiary title).

question: Several investors form a limited liability company (LLC) to purchase and hold title to an apartment building. Which statement best describes this ownership arrangement?
choice_a: Each individual member automatically holds direct fee simple title to a proportional share of the building
choice_b: The LLC, as a separate legal entity, holds title to the property, and its members generally receive limited personal liability protection from the entity's debts and obligations
choice_c: An LLC cannot legally hold title to real property
choice_d: Members of an LLC always have unlimited personal liability for property debts, the same as a general partnership
explanation: A limited liability company is a business entity that can hold title to real property in its own name. One of its key advantages is that members generally receive limited personal liability for the entity's debts and obligations, unlike general partners in a general partnership.
source_note: National ownership forms — business entity (LLC) ownership of real property.
